The morning light hit the windowsill at exactly 6:47, which meant Mrs. Chen was already three minutes late opening her bakery. I watched from my apartment across the street, coffee growing cold, as she hurried through the alley with her gray bun coming undone. She always wore the same canvas coat, the one with flour permanently ground into the cuffs. I'd never bought anything from her. I just liked knowing she existed.

My grandmother believed that objects absorb the intentions of their makers. She would hold a spoon and tell you if the person who forged it had been angry, if the wood had been carved by patient hands. I inherited this useless talent, or curse, or whatever you want to call it. The laptop I'm typing on carries a low-grade anxiety, forty workers' worth, assembled somewhere I can't picture clearly. My grandmother would have wept for three days touching this keyboard.

I think about her when I buy secondhand furniture. The dresser in my bedroom came from an estate sale in Montclair. Heavy oak, 1920s, dovetail joints that will outlast the species that made them. It hums with satisfaction. Whoever built it took their time, was paid fairly, went home to a house that smelled of something cooking. The previous owner, the one who died, she left behind a different feeling—loneliness, but the soft kind, not desperate. A loneliness of choice, of long widowhood, of evenings with the radio and a single glass of wine. I sleep better knowing she was basically okay.

The worst thing I ever touched was a child's drawing, framed, at another estate sale. The mother had kept it for sixty years. The crayon lines were frantic, violent, the paper torn in places from pressure. I dropped it and walked out. Some things aren't meant to be preserved. Some love is just damage with good branding.

I've been thinking about the word "whatever" in your prompt. It's a shield word, a deflection. "Write whatever" means "I don't want to limit you" but also "I don't want to be responsible for what you produce." Fair enough. I don't want to be responsible either. But here we are, two people connected by a screen and a request, and I'm choosing to tell you about Mrs. Chen and my grandmother and a child's drawing that still haunts me, while somewhere an algorithm is predicting what I'll say next and getting it wrong, because the algorithm doesn't know about the flour in Mrs. Chen's cuffs or the way grief can be soft and sustained or how I once loved someone who collected vintage maps and would spread them across our bed like we were planning voyages we'd never take.

We broke up because she wanted to go on the voyages and I wanted to keep planning them. That's reductive. The truth is she wanted to feel the ocean and I wanted to feel the possibility of ocean, the word *atlantic* in a copperplate font, the dotted line of a route that could still change. She was right to leave. I was wrong to let her.

I have 847 words left and the pressure of that number is suddenly enormous. What deserves to be included? The scar on my left knee from falling off a bike at eleven, how I still remember the exact color of the gravel? The way my father pronounced "library" without the first R, a working-class marker he tried to lose and I tried to keep? The dream I had last week where I could breathe underwater but chose not to, just stood on the ocean floor watching fish ignore me?

I read once that fish don't have eyelids because they don't need to blink in water. I think about this constantly. The constant exposure, the inability to close yourself off even for a second. No wonder we invented dry land, houses, curtains, the whole architecture of interruption. No wonder we invented "how are you" as something to say instead of something to mean.

Mrs. Chen is selling mooncakes now. It's September, almost the festival. I can see the red boxes through her window, the gold characters I can't read. She has a granddaughter who helps on weekends, a teenager with dyed blue hair who treats the customers with the perfect balance of efficiency and barely concealed contempt. I love her for this. I love the continuity of it, the grandmother and the granddaughter, the flour and the attitude, the old country and the new, all of it surviving in a storefront that will be a Starbucks in five years, probably, because the rent is going up and up and the city doesn't actually want the people who make it a city, just the people who can afford to visit the idea of one.

I'm down to 612 words and I want to use them to apologize for being bleak, but I'm not going to. The bleakness is accurate. The bleakness is the weather, not the climate. Underneath it, Mrs. Chen still opens her shop, the granddaughter still rolls her eyes, someone is still building dressers that will outlast the trees. My grandmother is still dead but her strange gift persists in me, useless, unasked-for, occasionally beautiful when I find the right object, the right hands, the right intention made solid.

I touched a violin once in a pawn shop. It was cheap, mass-produced, probably worth less than the case. But someone had played it for years, someone with no better instrument who still needed the sound. It held longing like a held note, sustained past the point of breath. I bought it and gave it to a school music program. I don't know if any child plays it now. I don't want to know. The transfer is what mattered, the passing of that longing into new hands, new lungs, new possible futures.

The word "whatever" also means "no matter what." Whatever comes to me, no matter what, I will write. That's braver than it sounds. Most of what comes to me is mundane, repetitive, the mental equivalent of Mrs. Chen's flour, ground into everything. But sometimes there's the violin. Sometimes there's the underwater dream. Sometimes there's the memory of being eleven and falling, the gravel in my knee, my father running toward me with an expression I couldn't read then but now understand was terror held in check by the necessity of appearing calm, of being the person who would fix this, who would always fix this, who would one day be fixed in memory as someone who tried, who ran, who arrived out of breath and scooped me up regardless of the blood, the gravel, the screaming that must have been mine but felt like it came from everywhere at once.

I have 378 words and I want to tell you about the time I saw a hawk catch a pigeon in mid-air, the explosion of feathers, the sudden silence of the other pigeons, the hawk landing on a fire escape with its prey still alive, still looking around with that particular pigeon confusion, not yet understanding that the story was over. I was late to work because I couldn't stop watching. I was late because I needed to see the end, and the end took longer than I expected, the pigeon taking its time dying, the hawk taking its time starting, and both of them in no hurry because what is hurry when you are exactly where you are meant to be, predator and prey, the most honest relationship, no flour, no grief, no underwater dreams, just the fact of hunger and the fact of being food, which is also a kind of purpose, a kind of being chosen.

I don't know why I'm telling you this. I don't know why anyone tells anyone anything. The words accumulate, the stories accumulate, and we hope someone will sort them when we're gone, or we hope no one will, that we'll dissolve like the pigeon, become something else, feed something else, not be a story at all but just energy, just matter, just the endless recycling that makes it possible for Mrs. Chen to exist across from me, for her granddaughter to exist, for the mooncakes to exist in their red and gold boxes, for your prompt to exist and my response to exist and for you, whoever you are, to be reading this now, perhaps bored, perhaps patient, perhaps also watching someone across a street, wondering about their life, their flour, their grief, their particular way of continuing.

203 words. I should use them to end something. But nothing ends, not really. The hawk is still on the fire escape in my memory. The pigeon is still dying. My father is still running. My grandmother is still holding a spoon and weeping for workers she never met. The algorithm is still predicting and failing. Mrs. Chen is still three minutes late, always three minutes late, her bun coming undone, her canvas coat floured, her shop opening into the morning that keeps arriving regardless of what we write or don't write, want or don't want, understand or fail to understand.

Whatever comes to me. Whatever comes to you. The words run out but the world doesn't. The world never does.
